title: Court blocks Trump administration plan to block funds for Planned Parenthood
summary: A federal judge has temporarily blocked a Trump administration plan to halt Medicaid funds for Planned Parenthood and similar health care providers.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 3, 2025

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 3, 2025

A federal judge has temporarily blocked a Trump administration plan to halt Medicaid funds for Planned Parenthood and similar health care providers.

The prelimnary injunction handed down Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts said a coalition of 22 Democratic attorneys general, including Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown, had “demonstrated a strong likelihood of success on the merits of their claim” that the denial of fund unconstitutionally attached conditions to congressionally approved spending without giving notice to the states.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote the law “is impermissibly ambiguous” and an “unprecedented incursion into States’ traditional discretion over the regulation of medicine that Plaintiff States could not have anticipated when joining Medicaid.”

Talwani also wrote if the administration kept this law in place, it “would increase the percentage of patients unable to receive birth control and preventive screenings, thereby prompting an increase in States’ healthcare costs.”

The plan to withhold Medicaid funding was part of an expansive tax and spending cuts package signed into law by President Donald Trump (R) on July 4. The law bans Medicaid funding for health care providers “primarily engaged in family planning services, reproductive health, and related medical care.”

Planned Parenthood Federation of America, along with two of its affiliates in Massachusetts and Utah, filed a lawsuit three days after Trump signed the tax cut and spending plan.

Justice Department sues six more states, including Maryland, for voter lists

Later in July, the states filed a lawsuit that challenged a provision that eliminates Medicaid reimbursements for one year to health care providers that provide abortions and received more than $800,000 in federal and state Medicaid funding in 2023.

The defendants listed in the suit are the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and its administrator, Mehmet Oz.

An HHS representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

Karen J. Nelson, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood of Maryland, released a statement Wednesday welcoming the court’s “recognition that this law is unconstitutional.”

“We offer our most sincere gratitude to the tireless work of Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown, who joined officials from 21 states and Washington, D.C. to fight against a ‘defund’ provision that will inevitably harm patients seeking crucial health care services,” she said.

The judge granted seven days for the Trump administration to appeal her ruling.

The Planned Parenthood lawsuit is just one of more than 100 legal actions – briefs and lawsuits – that the Maryland Attorney General’s Office has joined or led this year against the Trump administration. About four more were filed in November, including an amicus brief in support of California’s motion to dismiss a federal lawsuit that demands unredacted voter registration databases.

Brown, who serves as a co-led on the brief with 15 other attorneys general, argues in the brief the federal government seeks to collect personal information nationwide.

“Maryland voters deserve to cast ballots without worrying that their registration information will be mishandled,” Brown said in a statement. “The administration’s unlawful demands threaten both individual privacy and our collective confidence in our elections. We won’t allow federal overreach to undermine voting rights or discourage participation in our democracy.”
